disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by a continuous period of illness during which a major depressive episode co-occurs with symptoms of schizophrenia, such as delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized thinking. Crucially, there must be at least two weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features, while mood episodes are present for the majority of the total illness duration, differentiating it from schizophrenia. The course is often chronic or recurrent, with variable degrees of functional impairment in work, social relationships, and self-care, and it may be preceded by a period of increasing stress, social withdrawal, and subtle cognitive or perceptual changes. Onset typically occurs in late adolescence to mid-adulthood but can emerge later in life, often in the context of genetic vulnerability interacting with psychosocial stressors such as losses, health changes, or occupational strain.

narrative.personality: Zoila is a practical, community-minded problem-solver who enjoys hands-on projects, mentoring others, and staying busy with sports, gardening, and DIY tinkering.
narrative.stressor: The onset of Zoila’s difficulties followed a year when her maintenance department at a large housing complex became chronically understaffed, leaving her covering emergency call-outs at all hours while also being pushed into an unofficial lead role. At the same time, she took on extra side jobs doing green-renovation work to help her and her spouse save for a house, leaving little time for rest, soccer, or her usual grounding routines like gardening and tinkering with radios. Over many months, the relentless pressure, irregular hours, and sense that she was solely responsible for keeping buildings and tenants safe eroded her usual resilience, and she began to feel increasingly isolated, worn down, and preoccupied by work even at home. As her functioning slipped—missing minor safety checks, snapping at junior techs she normally mentored patiently, and withdrawing from community activities—her sleep became so disrupted and her thinking so unsettled that her spouse insisted she see a doctor, leading to psychiatric referral when it became clear her distress and unusual experiences had been ongoing for nearly two years.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t sleep through the night anymore, and even when I do sleep, it doesn’t feel restful.”

narrative.personality: Ashley is a meticulous yet imaginative person who balances her love of numbers with a deep passion for creative arts and community involvement.
narrative.stressor: Ashley’s condition emerged gradually after the unexpected death of her older sister, who had been her closest confidante and main emotional support throughout her divorce and midlife transitions. In the months following the loss, Ashley threw herself into volunteer treasurer duties and new art projects, trying to stay busy, but she found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on her bookkeeping job and her evenings alone at home felt unbearably empty. Over time, she became more withdrawn from her book club and theater group, spending long hours in her apartment painting and ruminating about whether she could have prevented her sister’s death, while her inner world grew more intense and began to intrude on her day-to-day functioning. When she started reacting in distress to experiences she could not easily explain, and her coworkers and arts council colleagues noticed marked changes in her reliability and demeanor over nearly two years, a concerned friend from the community theater accompanied her to a primary care visit, which led to psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been hearing things that no one else seems to hear, and it’s starting to really scare me.”

narrative.personality: Robert is an intellectually curious, creative former engineer who enjoys mentoring, artistic pursuits, and community activities, though he tends to keep a flexible and somewhat disorganized routine.
narrative.stressor: Robert’s difficulties began after a minor stroke scare and subsequent cardiac workup two years ago, which, although ultimately reassuring in terms of immediate danger, forced him to confront his mortality more directly than ever before. He cut back on some adjunct teaching and museum work at his family’s urging, which left him with fewer structured roles and more unoccupied time, disrupting the sense of purpose he had long derived from mentoring and building projects. As he spent more time alone at home, alternating between painting, reading, and ruminating about his life’s arc, he became increasingly preoccupied with aging, decline, and the possibility of becoming a burden to his spouse, and his thinking about death slowly shifted from philosophical curiosity to something darker and more fixed. Over the following year and a half, his wife and fellow seniors at the chess club noticed he seemed more withdrawn and occasionally spoke in a way that suggested he was struggling to distinguish his fears and internal experiences from reality, prompting his family doctor—concerned by the persistence and depth of his morbid preoccupations—to refer him for psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been thinking a lot about dying and sometimes I wonder if everyone would be better off if I just weren’t here.”
